questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.topic: Relativistic momentum of a fast electron
questions.learningObjective: Compute relativistic momentum of an electron at high speed
questions.stem: A field biologist's survey scenario treats an electron moving at 0.99c, and asks for the factor by which its relativistic momentum exceeds the classical value

options.text: About 7 because gamma is roughly 7 at 0.99c
About 1 because momentum is invariant
options.misconception: assumes momentum does not increase with speed

options.text: About 0.01 because the electron is nearly massless
options.misconception: confuses relativistic momentum with rest mass

options.text: About 100 because speed near c multiplies momentum by 100

questions.explanation: Relativistic momentum is gamma times m v, so at 0.99c with gamma about 7.09, the momentum exceeds the classical value by roughly 7. The classical formula misses the gamma factor.
questions.hint: Momentum gains a factor of gamma at high speed.

questions.stem: A field biologist's survey scenario gives an electron kinetic energy of 1 MeV, and asks which formula yields the correct speed

options.text: K equals one half m v squared from classical mechanics
options.misconception: uses classical kinetic energy near light speed

options.text: K equals (gamma minus 1) m c squared from relativity
K equals gamma m c squared ignoring the rest energy
options.misconception: uses total energy instead of kinetic energy

options.text: K equals m c squared over gamma

questions.explanation: Relativistic kinetic energy is (gamma minus 1) m c squared. The classical formula fails when speeds approach c, and total energy includes the rest energy.
questions.hint: Subtract rest energy from total energy.

options.misconception: uses c instead of c squared

questions.explanation: Rest energy E equals m c squared, so 9.11e-31 kg times (3e8 m/s)^2 gives about 8.19e-14 J. This is the energy equivalent of the electron's mass.
